UK sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of its obligations, legal experts say
article.full_text: More than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel (KCs), have written to Andy Burnham saying that sanctions on Israeli settlements “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under the international court of justice’s (ICJ’s) finding that the occupation is unlawful. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last week announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine and other measures. Signatories to the letter to the prime minister, including the leading lawyers Michael Mansfield KC and Imran Khan KC, and the former lord justice of appeal Alan Moses, say it is not enough. In a 2024 advisory opinion, the ICJ, which is the UN’s top court, ordered Israel to end the occupation “as rapidly as possible” and said other countries were under an obligation not to recognise the occupation as lawful nor aid or assist it. The letter, sent on Tuesday, says the ICJ’s findings have “not had an impact on Israel’s apartheid practice” and, while the UK sanctions are “a necessary corrective”, they are “improperly narrow” when compared with sanctions on Russia, which are not limited to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory but apply to wider economic structures supporting the unlawful conduct. It says: “We ask it to commit to further and more rigorous measures to ensure that no part of the UK’s economic relationship with Israel continues to sustain the illegal occupation itself, and the settlements and other serious violations of fundamental rules of international law perpetrated through its conduct, and to build on this to adopt robust coercive measures to seek to bring all these serious violations of international law, and the practices they sustain, including, fundamentally, the occupation itself, to an end.” The letter, also signed by legal academics, calls for a range of additional measures including a full arms embargo on Israel. When announcing the sanctions, Miliband accused Israel of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and the signatories say article 6(3) of the arms trade treaty prohibits transfers of arms where a state has knowledge of such a crime. The sanctions were announced after escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender was issued for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement, east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state. The signatories want extension of the sanctions to cover insurance, accountancy services and digital infrastructure as well as public confirmation that no UK public body, pension scheme or sovereign fund holds settlement investments. One of the letter’s signatories and drafters, Ralph Wilde, a professor of international law at University College London, welcomed the UK’s recent recognition of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as unlawful as an “important shift”, but said it fell short in its focus on the settlements and settlers. “The elephant in the room is the illegality of the occupation itself,” said Wilde, who acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in the case before the ICJ. “It’s not just simply the settlements and the abuse of treatment and the genocide, which of course are also wrong, it’s Israel’s very presence.” He added: “There’s a mismatch between saying Israel’s very presence there is illegal, but then only focusing on the question of the settlers and the settlements. If the problem is with the settlements themselves, then the problem is with the state that establishes them.” A government spokesperson said: “This is the biggest reset in the UK’s approach to protecting and securing the two-state solution in a generation. UK ministers urged to act after US flies out diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children
article.full_text: British ministers face calls to act after US authorities secretly flew out of the UK a diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children. US officials reportedly raided the diplomat’s London flat in August before taking him to an American airbase and flying him out of the country, without warning the Metropolitan police. American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain, and there was no formal request for the man to be extradited. UK ministers are understood to be in contact with the US embassy over the incident, which could further strain relations between London and Washington. Elements of the case echo that of an American fighter pilot, first reported in the Guardian, who avoided being tried under English law for strangling a woman in Cambridge while off-duty. Capt Jacob Wulfson was tried by court martial at a US airbase and jailed for six months after being convicted of strangulation. He was acquitted of charges of sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact. In a letter to the justice secretary, Alex Norris, his Conservative counterpart, Nick Timothy, said he was concerned US actions represented “a cover-up” and that the diplomat may have committed offences in the UK. “If this is the case, the diplomat should face trial in an English court.” Timothy said the incident was part of a “concerning pattern” of US authorities prosecuting American service personnel accused of offences against British civilians while stationed in the UK. Citing the Wulfson case, he wrote: “These cases should have been investigated by the English police and prosecuted in our courts. I ask you to urgently explain what action you are taking to address this, and what will be done to ensure the accused diplomat faces a proper investigation in this country.” The diplomat’s case has also been likened to that of the US state department employee Anne Sacoolas, who caused the death of the teenager Harry Dunn in a car crash in 2019. Sacoolas was able to leave the country shortly after the fatal collision when the US asserted diplomatic immunity on her behalf. She eventually pleaded guilty to causing death by careless driving at a virtual high-court hearing in December 2022, and was sentenced to eight months in prison, suspended for a year. A UK government spokesperson declined to comment because of the ongoing US investigation but said Britain expects all foreign diplomats to obey the law while in the UK, “in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas”. A spokesperson for the US embassy said it was “aware of allegations” concerning one of its staff and expected “all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct”. The spokesperson said: “We quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action, and we will continue to work closely with our law enforcement partners regarding these allegations. “The individual in question has been reassigned to the United States in conjunction with an ongoing investigation. The embassy has informed British authorities of the case.” A US state department spokesperson declined to discuss the specifics of the case, adding: “We take these allegations seriously.” A Met police spokesperson said: “On Tuesday 25 August, US authorities made us aware of an investigation they are conducting into suspected offences in London relating to indecent images of children. We continue to liaise with them regarding this matter.”
